records.title: Decompression sickness: an increasing risk for the private pilot

case_profile.retrospective_diagnosis: Authors favored altitude DCS. Original hospital working diagnosis was cerebellar ataxia of unknown origin.

observations.protocol: Unpressurized private-aircraft flight to FL250. The pilot reported starting oxygen by nasal cannula passing FL110 and changing to a rebreather mask passing FL180. Actual oxygen dose and complete cabin pressure history were unavailable.
observations.outcome_window: Initial symptoms approximately 45 minutes into cruise. Later neurological review was at three months. Some deficits reportedly persisted for several years.
observations.locator: Case Report, pp. 200–201 and Discussion p. 201
observations.note: One retrospectively attributed episode. In-flight abdominal and shoulder pain preceded focal and visual symptoms and loss of consciousness during descent. Initial hospital diagnosis was cerebellar ataxia of unknown origin. No hyperbaric therapy was administered.

milestones.note: Abdominal cramps and left shoulder pain, followed by numbness.
Visual blurring occurred within five minutes of the first symptoms.
Symptoms worsened when descent began. An exact altitude or elapsed time for loss of consciousness was not reported.

milestones.elapsed_reference: elapsed at FL190 after descent began
milestones.note: The patient remained unconscious during the stated 30-minute hold due to terrain.
At three months after the incident, neurological abnormalities remained. No hyperbaric therapy was given.
Ongoing cognitive and night-vision symptoms were described over several subsequent years without an exact interval.

records.note: Original report of one selected civilian pilot. The authors retrospectively favor DCS and the original treating team did not make that diagnosis. Event date and exposure denominator are unavailable.

records.title: Decompression sickness in a private pilot
records.full_text_version: Author-attributed public transcription. Publisher PDF access is restricted.

case_profile.residual_deficit: Mild right shoulder weakness at follow-up.

observations.protocol: Unpressurized private-aircraft flight at 28,000 ft MSL. The pilot reported using supplemental oxygen above 12,000 ft and continued oxygen during descent. Actual oxygen delivery, prebreathe and the complete profile were unavailable.
observations.outcome_window: First symptoms after one hour at cruise. Chamber therapy started approximately 12 hours after landing. Follow-up reported at one year.
observations.note: One author-diagnosed altitude DCS episode. New right arm weakness and paresthesias preceded bilateral symptoms. The patient received an initial compression treatment and seven further treatments, with mild residual right shoulder weakness at the one-year assessment.

milestones.note: Right arm weakness and paresthesias, followed by fatigue, chest tightness, dry cough and left arm symptoms.
Compression began immediately after arrival at Brooks, about 12 hours after landing.
Seven further treatments were administered, with improvement after five and no further improvement after the last two.
One-year review showed recovery of right-hand muscle function and persistent mild right shoulder weakness.

records.note: Public author-attributed case transcription corroborated by a matching copy and the indexed author abstract. The publisher journal pages were inaccessible. The digest is for the exact HTML transcription. Event date and exposure denominator are unavailable.

records.title: Neurologic decompression sickness following cabin pressure fluctuations at high altitude
records.locator: Introduction p. 427 and Case Study pp. 427–428

observations.protocol: Reported 12 cabin-pressure cycles between 18,000 and 38,000 ft cabin altitude while the aircraft was at FL430. After descent the aircraft flew at FL240 with cabin altitude reported as 8,000 ft. The case narrative says three minutes of cycling, and the introduction describes a ten-minute period.
observations.outcome_window: Symptoms about one hour after the cabin fluctuations. First hyperbaric treatment about 3.5 hours after those fluctuations. Follow-up at one year.
observations.locator: Introduction p. 427 and Case Study pp. 427–428
observations.note: One symptomatic pilot with clinical suspicion favoring neurological DCS. The individual cycles, complete gas history and actual start and end pressures are unavailable. The author abstract and case study do not establish an exposure denominator.

milestones.note: Aircraft flight level, not cabin pressure altitude.

milestones.elapsed_reference: cycling duration in the case study
milestones.locator: Introduction p. 427 and Case Study p. 428
milestones.note: The case study reports 12 cycles between 18,000 and 38,000 ft cabin altitude during the next three minutes. The introduction instead mentions a ten-minute period.
Felt unwell, then reported lightheadedness, fatigue and confusion. Aircraft was at FL240 after descent and cabin altitude had stabilized near 8,000 ft.
Emergency team documented asymmetric weakness, sensory changes and confusion.

milestones.locator: Abstract p. 427 and Case Study p. 428
milestones.note: The authors separately report 2.5 hours from symptom onset. Treatment used US Navy Table 6.
The patient reported some relief by 30 minutes and complete resolution by 90 minutes.
The pilot remained asymptomatic at day 16. At the reported one-year review he was symptom-free.

records.note: Original report of one selected tactical pilot with suspected neurological DCS. Dates of exposure and exact cabin pressure trace are unreported. Individual flights or exposed aircrew counts are unavailable.

records.title: Decompression sickness in a private pilot
records.note: The byline and author summary identify Rudge's article. The 59-year-old pilot, 28,000 ft cruise, 12-hour postlanding treatment and one-year outcome match the clinical transcription. This version supplies no separate case.
